## Fakhr al-Din al-Razi: Philosophy, Theology, Tafsir & Avicenna

**Source URL:** https://agnostickind.github.io/philosophy-website/fakhr-al-din-al-razi.html

## Who Was Fakhr al-Din al-Razi?

**Fakhr al-Din al-Razi** (Abū ʿAbdillāh Muḥammad ibn
ʿUmar al-Rāzī, 1149–1210 CE) was one of the most influential and
intellectually innovative theologians, philosophers, and scholars of
the medieval Islamic world. He is especially known for his rigorous
and often critical engagement with
**Avicenna's philosophy**, his major role in the later
development of **Ash'ari theology**
(*kalam*), and his monumental Quranic commentary,
*Mafatih al-Ghayb*, commonly known as the
**Tafsir al-Kabir**.

Al-Razi was trained from an early age in Islamic theology and law and
became deeply familiar with the philosophical tradition associated
with
**Avicenna (Ibn Sina)**. Rather than simply accepting or
rejecting Avicennian philosophy, he examined its arguments critically
and contributed to debates concerning metaphysics, logic, physics, the
human soul, knowledge, ethics, and the relationship between essence
and existence. His philosophical writings helped shape what later
scholars describe as the post-classical development of Islamic
thought.

Much of Al-Razi's intellectual importance lies in his willingness to
bring different traditions into sustained debate. He used
philosophical methods in theological argument while also subjecting
philosophical claims to rigorous criticism. This approach helped
transform **kalam**
during the centuries after Al-Ghazali and contributed to the
increasingly close interaction between philosophy, logic, and theology
in the eastern Islamic world.

Al-Razi was also an extraordinarily prolific author whose interests
extended beyond theology and philosophy. His surviving works address
Quranic interpretation, Islamic law, logic, natural philosophy,
medicine, astronomy, and other fields. His writings were widely
studied and debated, and his influence continued through later
traditions of Islamic theology and philosophy long after his death in
Herat in 1210 CE.

**Note:** Fakhr al-Din al-Razi should not be confused
with the earlier physician and philosopher
**Abu Bakr al-Razi**, known in Latin as
**Rhazes**, who died in the early tenth century. The two
were distinct thinkers from different historical periods, although
both were associated through their names with the Persian city of
Rayy.

## Fakhr al-Din al-Razi: Quick Facts

- **Full name** — Abū ʿAbdillāh Muḥammad ibn ʿUmar
  al-Rāzī
- **Known as** — Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, or Ibn al-Khatib
- **Born** — 1149 CE, Rayy, in present-day Iran
- **Died** — 1210 CE, Herat, in present-day Afghanistan
- **Associated with** — Rayy, Khwarazm, Transoxiana, and
  Herat
- **Philosophical tradition** — Ash'ari theology (kalam),
  critical engagement with Avicennan Peripatetic philosophy
- **Legal school** — Shafi'i jurisprudence
- **Major philosophical subjects** — Theology,
  metaphysics, logic, epistemology, atomism, and Quranic exegesis
- **Famous exegetical work** —
  *Tafsir al-Kabir* (Mafatih al-Ghayb)
- **Famous critical work** — Commentary on Avicenna's
  *Remarks and Admonitions*
- **Not to be confused with** — Abu Bakr al-Razi
  (Rhazes), an earlier physician-philosopher

## Al-Razi's Early Life and Historical Background

[Image: Representation of Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, Islamic theologian and philosopher]

Fakhr al-Din al-Razi became one of the most encyclopedic and
influential scholars of the medieval Islamic world.

Fakhr al-Din al-Razi was born in 1149 CE in **Rayy**, the
important Persian city near modern Tehran from which his name
*al-Razi* was derived. He was born into a family deeply
involved in religious scholarship. His father, Diya al-Din Umar, was
associated with Ash'ari theology and Shafi'i jurisprudence, and
Al-Razi therefore received an early education in Islamic law, rational
theology, Arabic, and the methods of religious argument.

His education later expanded beyond his family's scholarly tradition.
Al-Razi studied at **Nishapur**, where he encountered the
philosophical works of thinkers such as Al-Farabi and
**Avicenna (Ibn Sina)**, whose philosophy would become
the central object of his critical engagement. He also studied with
Majd al-Din al-Jili at Maragha, entering an intellectual environment
in which philosophy and theology were increasingly studied alongside
one another.

Al-Razi subsequently traveled widely through Persia and Central Asia
in search of education, patronage, and intellectual opponents. His
career was shaped by the political rivalry between the Khwarazm-Shahs
and the Ghurids, and he gained a reputation as an exceptionally
formidable teacher and debater. These travels brought him into contact
with different theological, philosophical, and political communities
across the eastern Islamic world.

During his mature career, Al-Razi enjoyed important patronage and
eventually became associated with the Ghurid court. Despite his
political and intellectual travels, he produced an extraordinarily
large body of writing covering philosophy, theology, logic, Islamic
law, Quranic interpretation, natural philosophy, medicine, and
subjects such as astrology. He died in
**Herat in 1210 CE**, leaving behind one of the most
extensive intellectual legacies of the post-classical Islamic world.

## Al-Razi and Ash'ari Theology (Kalam)

Al-Razi is one of the major figures in the history of
**Ash'ari theology**, the influential tradition of Sunni
rational theology known as **kalam**. He inherited an
Ash'ari intellectual background through his father and through the
scholarly tradition associated with the earlier theologian Imam
al-Juwayni. Yet his own theological writings developed in an age when
Ash'ari scholars were engaging increasingly closely with the
philosophical tradition of Avicenna.

Al-Razi did not treat theology and philosophy as completely isolated
disciplines. He incorporated philosophical distinctions, logical
methods, and technical forms of argument into theological discussion,
while also challenging philosophical conclusions that he regarded as
insufficiently demonstrated. This helped produce a more
philosophically sophisticated form of kalam, often associated by
modern scholars with the development of
**later kalam**.

His theological works examine questions concerning God's existence and
attributes, creation, causation, prophecy, the human soul, knowledge,
and the physical structure of the world. Al-Razi frequently presented
multiple competing arguments before examining their strengths and
weaknesses, which means that his writings cannot always be reduced to
a single simple doctrinal position.

The long-term importance of Al-Razi lies partly in this transformation
of theological method. After him, later Islamic theologians
increasingly worked with philosophical vocabulary and argumentative
techniques that had previously been associated primarily with
**falsafa**. His writings therefore became a major
meeting point between Ash'ari theology and the philosophical
traditions inherited from Aristotle and Avicenna.

## Al-Razi's Critique of Avicenna

One of Al-Razi's most important philosophical activities was his
sustained engagement with the thought of **Avicenna**. He
wrote an influential commentary on Avicenna's
*Remarks and Admonitions* (*al-Isharat wa al-Tanbihat*),
one of the great philosophical texts of the Islamic intellectual
tradition. His engagement with Avicenna was unusually detailed and
helped make Avicennan philosophy the subject of a new generation of
critical philosophical debate.

Al-Razi did not simply reject Avicenna from the standpoint of
theology. Instead, he often examined Avicennan arguments on their own
philosophical terms. His writings raise objections concerning
metaphysics, the possibility of real definitions, the distinction
between essence and existence, the principles of natural philosophy,
the nature and unity of the human soul, and other central elements of
the Avicennan system.

This critical method is one reason why Al-Razi occupies such an
important place in the history of post-classical Islamic philosophy.
He treated Avicenna as an intellectual opponent whose arguments
required serious and technical answers rather than rhetorical
dismissal. At the same time, his enormous corpus contains substantial
engagement with Avicennan concepts, and his own positions sometimes
developed over the course of his career.

Al-Razi's relationship to Avicenna should therefore not be described
simply as rejection or acceptance. His philosophical career helped
transform the Avicennan tradition by forcing later thinkers to
confront objections that were formulated from within the highly
technical language of philosophy itself. Later commentators, including
Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, would continue this debate and respond directly
to Al-Razi's criticisms.

## Al-Razi's Arguments for the Existence of God

Al-Razi devoted extensive attention to arguments concerning the
existence of God. He inherited both the philosophical tradition of
Avicenna and the theological arguments developed within kalam, and his
writings frequently compare different methods rather than presenting
only one unquestioned proof as sufficient for every philosophical
purpose.

A central philosophical argument available to Al-Razi was Avicenna's
analysis of **necessary and contingent existence**.
According to this general framework, contingent beings do not contain
within themselves the complete explanation of their existence and
therefore depend ultimately upon a being whose existence is necessary
rather than contingent. Al-Razi examined this tradition closely while
raising objections to aspects of Avicennan metaphysics.

He also considered arguments associated with kalam, particularly
arguments based on the dependence or created character of the world
and the need for an explanatory cause beyond contingent physical
reality. Discussions of infinite causal regress, temporal beginning,
motion, and the composition of bodies all formed part of the broader
medieval debate about how philosophical reasoning could establish the
existence of a Creator.

Al-Razi's importance in this field lies less in the invention of a
single universally named proof than in his comparative and critical
treatment of several competing arguments. His discussions became an
important resource for later theologians and philosophers seeking to
determine which forms of reasoning could provide the strongest
demonstration of God's existence.

[Image: Conceptual illustration of atomism in medieval Islamic theology and philosophy]

Al-Razi engaged closely with debates over atomism, continuity, and
the physical structure of the world.

## Al-Razi's Philosophy of Atomism

Atomism was an important subject within medieval
**kalam**. Many theologians defended the view that
physical bodies are ultimately composed of indivisible units or atoms
together with changing properties often described as accidents. This
account differed sharply from the Aristotelian and Avicennan
understanding of bodies in terms of matter, form, continuity, and
potentially infinite divisibility.

Al-Razi examined these competing theories in considerable technical
detail. He engaged with Avicenna's criticisms of kalam atomism and
considered questions concerning magnitude, divisibility, motion,
continuity, and the actual structure of physical bodies. His work
therefore belongs to a major medieval debate about whether
mathematical continuity accurately represents the structure of
reality.

His position also appears to have developed across his writings.
Modern scholarship has emphasized that Al-Razi's views cannot always
be represented by a single unchanging doctrine, and his later works
show stronger engagement with physical atomism and arguments
concerning limits to divisibility. This makes his treatment more
complex than a simple repetition of earlier Ash'ari positions.

Al-Razi's discussions of atomism are historically important because
they helped transmit and transform debates between
**kalam** and **falsafa**. They show him
working at the boundary between theological conceptions of creation
and sophisticated philosophical questions concerning mathematics,
physical extension, and the nature of material reality.

## Al-Razi's Tafsir al-Kabir (Mafatih al-Ghayb)

Al-Razi's most famous work is his monumental Quranic commentary,
***Mafatih al-Ghayb***, usually translated as *Keys to the Unseen*. It later became
widely known as the ***Tafsir al-Kabir***, or *The Great Commentary*. Its extraordinary size and
intellectual range made it one of the most important works of Quranic
interpretation in the Islamic tradition.

The commentary is remarkable for the range of questions it
incorporates into the interpretation of Quranic passages. Al-Razi
discusses theology, metaphysics, logic, natural philosophy, cosmology,
ethics, language, and legal questions alongside more conventional
forms of Quranic exegesis. Individual verses often become starting
points for extended philosophical and theological investigations.

This does not mean that Al-Razi abandoned the traditional concerns of
exegesis. Linguistic interpretation, theological tradition, and the
relationship between verses remain important throughout the work. What
makes his commentary distinctive is the way these concerns are
combined with the intellectual debates of his own age, producing an
encyclopedic form of scriptural interpretation.

*Mafatih al-Ghayb* became enormously influential and was
studied by later scholars across different regions of the Islamic
world. It remains essential for understanding how philosophy and
rational theology could be incorporated into Quranic commentary and
demonstrates the unusually broad intellectual range of Al-Razi's
scholarship.

## Al-Razi's Logic and Epistemology

Logic played a central role in Al-Razi's intellectual method. Like
many post-Avicennan thinkers, he treated logical analysis as an
essential tool for testing arguments in philosophy and theology. Yet
he was not satisfied simply to repeat the inherited Aristotelian and
Avicennan tradition, and his writings contain important criticisms
concerning definition, conceptual knowledge, and the conditions
required for genuine demonstration.

One of his significant philosophical concerns was the problem of
**real definitions**. Al-Razi questioned whether human
beings can always grasp the essential nature of things through the
kinds of definitions demanded by traditional Aristotelian logic. This
criticism raised wider epistemological questions about the limits of
conceptual analysis and the relationship between words, concepts, and
reality.

His epistemological discussions also reflect a broader intellectual
habit: he frequently presents several possible arguments, objections,
and replies before reaching a conclusion—or, in some cases, leaving
the question open. This method can make his writings demanding, but it
also reveals his commitment to examining the strength of an argument
rather than merely defending inherited authority.

Al-Razi's influence on later logic and epistemology was therefore
closely connected with his critical method. He helped establish an
intellectual environment in which Avicennan logical concepts continued
to dominate scholarly debate while also becoming subjects of
increasingly sophisticated criticism and revision.

## Al-Razi's Philosophy of Ethics and Human Nature

Al-Razi did not construct a single ethical system comparable in form
to Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics* or Miskawayh's
*Tahdhib al-Akhlaq*. Nevertheless, ethical questions appear
throughout his philosophical, theological, and exegetical writings,
particularly in his discussions of human action, moral responsibility,
happiness, suffering, divine justice, and the foundations of ethical
norms.

One of the major questions connected with his ethical thought concerns
the source of moral value. Medieval Islamic theologians and
philosophers debated whether reason could independently know that
actions were good or bad, or whether moral obligation depended
fundamentally upon divine command. Al-Razi engaged with these debates
while also examining philosophical arguments concerning human nature
and rational judgment.

Questions concerning human freedom were equally important. As an
Ash'ari theologian, Al-Razi worked within a tradition strongly
concerned with the relationship between divine omnipotence and human
responsibility. His discussions explore how human actions can be
attributed to individuals while remaining within a world understood as
dependent upon divine power and causation.

Al-Razi's ethical thought is therefore best understood as distributed
throughout a larger intellectual project rather than confined to one
independent ethical treatise. His writings connect morality with
metaphysics, theology, psychology, and Quranic interpretation,
reflecting the integrated character of medieval Islamic philosophy and
theology.

## Major Works of Fakhr al-Din al-Razi

Al-Razi was an exceptionally prolific author. His works range across
theology, philosophy, logic, Islamic law, Quranic interpretation,
natural philosophy, and other disciplines, although the enormous size
of his corpus and the history of manuscript transmission make the
precise classification and chronology of some works a subject of
scholarly research.

- ***Mafatih al-Ghayb* (Tafsir al-Kabir)**
  — Al-Razi's monumental Quranic commentary, integrating exegesis with
  theology, philosophy, natural inquiry, language, and other
  intellectual disciplines.
- **Commentary on Avicenna's *Remarks and Admonitions* (*Sharh al-Isharat wa al-Tanbihat*)**
  — A major and highly influential critical engagement with Avicenna's
  philosophical arguments.
- ***al-Mabahith al-Mashriqiyya* ("Eastern Investigations")**
  — An extensive philosophical work addressing questions in
  metaphysics and natural philosophy.
- ***al-Muhassal***
  — A systematic work surveying important theological and
  philosophical positions and arguments.
- ***al-Mahsul***
  — A major contribution to the principles and methodology of Islamic
  jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*).
- ***al-Arba'in fi Usul al-Din* ("Forty Issues in Theology")**
  — A substantial theological work examining central questions
  concerning God, theology, and religious doctrine.
- ***Asas al-Taqdis***
  — An important theological work associated with debates concerning
  the divine attributes and the interpretation of anthropomorphic
  language.

## Fakhr al-Din al-Razi's Main Philosophical Ideas

### 1. Rigorous Testing of Philosophical Claims

Al-Razi subjected even highly authoritative philosophical arguments,
especially those associated with Avicenna, to detailed critical
examination. His method frequently involved presenting an argument,
raising objections, considering possible replies, and testing whether
the conclusion genuinely followed from its premises.

### 2. The Meeting of Kalam and Falsafa

Al-Razi helped bring rational theology and philosophical argument into
increasingly close contact. He used philosophical concepts within
kalam while also challenging philosophical doctrines through
theological and logical criticism, helping shape the intellectual
style of later Islamic thought.

### 3. The Limits of Definition and Conceptual Knowledge

A distinctive part of Al-Razi's philosophical criticism concerns the
possibility of defining things by their essential nature. His doubts
about traditional theories of definition raised broader questions
about how far conceptual analysis can provide certain knowledge of
reality.

### 4. Competing Arguments for God's Existence

Al-Razi compared philosophical and theological approaches to
demonstrating God's existence. Rather than relying exclusively on one
method, he examined arguments based on contingency, causation,
creation, the structure of the world, and the dependence of contingent
beings.

### 5. Critical Engagement with Atomism and Physics

Al-Razi investigated competing accounts of physical reality, including
atomism and Aristotelian theories of matter and form. His discussions
of divisibility and continuity illustrate his willingness to connect
theological questions with technical problems in mathematics and
natural philosophy.

### 6. Philosophy Within Quranic Interpretation

Through *Mafatih al-Ghayb*, Al-Razi demonstrated how
philosophical and theological debate could become part of Quranic
exegesis. His commentary treats scripture not only as a religious text
to be explained, but also as a starting point for broad intellectual
investigation.

## Al-Razi's Late-Life Doubt and Intellectual Humility

Al-Razi is traditionally associated with passages expressing deep
intellectual frustration about the limits of speculative reasoning.
Later readers have often connected these statements with the idea
that, near the end of his life, he became increasingly aware of the
difficulty of reaching complete certainty through philosophical and
theological argument alone.

One famous sentiment attributed to him expresses disappointment with
the results of extensive intellectual investigation and is often
translated in ways suggesting that the efforts of great thinkers had
led largely to perplexity or uncertainty. Such passages became
important in later discussions of Al-Razi's intellectual development
and his attitude toward philosophical speculation.

These statements should, however, be interpreted cautiously. Medieval
biographical reports and later quotations do not automatically provide
a simple account of a final conversion away from philosophy or a
complete rejection of rational inquiry. Al-Razi continued to be
remembered precisely as one of the most technically sophisticated
philosophical theologians of his age.

The most defensible interpretation is therefore one of
**intellectual humility** rather than a simple
abandonment of philosophy. Throughout his writings, Al-Razi repeatedly
exposes weaknesses in arguments that others considered decisive, and
his awareness of the limits of human certainty forms part of the same
critical intellectual temperament that made his work so influential.

## Al-Razi and Al-Ghazali: Two Approaches to Critiquing Philosophy

**Al-Razi and Al-Ghazali** were both major Sunni
theologians who engaged critically with philosophical traditions,
especially the philosophical legacy associated with Avicenna. Both
questioned whether particular metaphysical claims had been
successfully demonstrated and both considered the relationship between
philosophical reasoning and religious doctrine to be a central
intellectual problem.

Their methods, however, should not be reduced to a simple opposition
between rejection and acceptance. Al-Ghazali's
*Incoherence of the Philosophers*
is a sustained philosophical critique that often uses the conceptual
tools of the philosophers against their own conclusions. Al-Razi
inherited a later intellectual environment in which Avicennan
philosophy had become even more deeply integrated into scholarly
debate.

Al-Razi therefore engaged with Avicenna at an exceptionally technical
level, particularly through detailed commentaries and philosophical
summae. He examined individual arguments concerning metaphysics,
psychology, physics, logic, and epistemology rather than limiting his
attention to a small number of famous theological controversies.

The difference between the two thinkers is consequently best
understood as partly historical and methodological. Al-Ghazali was
crucial in reshaping the debate over philosophy, while Al-Razi became
one of the major figures who developed the intensely philosophical
form of kalam characteristic of later medieval Islamic intellectual
life.

## Al-Razi's Influence and Legacy

Al-Razi's influence on later Islamic theology and philosophy was
immense. His writings became major reference points for scholars
working in the intellectual traditions that developed after the
classical age of Avicenna. His combination of philosophical
sophistication, theological argument, and critical analysis helped
define important features of post-classical Islamic thought.

His engagement with Avicenna was especially consequential. Later
thinkers did not simply inherit Avicennan philosophy unchanged; they
also inherited the objections raised by Al-Razi. Philosophers such as
Nasir al-Din al-Tusi responded to his criticisms, ensuring that the
debate between Avicennan philosophy and its critics continued across
later centuries.

The influence of *Mafatih al-Ghayb* was equally extensive. Its
integration of theology, philosophy, natural inquiry, language, and
Quranic interpretation made it one of the great encyclopedic works of
the Islamic exegetical tradition and ensured Al-Razi's continuing
importance beyond specialist philosophical circles.

Al-Razi's legacy therefore cannot be confined to one discipline. He
was simultaneously a theologian, philosopher, logician, jurist,
commentator, and participant in debates about the natural world. His
work represents a crucial stage in the increasingly close interaction
between
**kalam, falsafa, logic, and Quranic scholarship**.

## Fakhr al-Din al-Razi's Philosophy Explained Simply

Al-Razi can be understood as a thinker who refused to accept an
argument simply because it came from a famous philosopher or an
established theological tradition. He studied both philosophy and
theology at the highest technical level and repeatedly asked whether
their arguments genuinely proved what they claimed to prove.

- **Was he a philosopher or a theologian?**
  Both. He was a major Ash'ari theologian who also became one of the
  most important philosophical critics and interpreters of the
  Avicennan tradition.
- **What did he think of Avicenna?**
  He took Avicenna extremely seriously but criticized many of his
  arguments in detail. His relationship to Avicennan philosophy was
  one of sustained engagement rather than simple acceptance or
  rejection.
- **What is he most famous for?**
  His enormous Quranic commentary, *Mafatih al-Ghayb*, also
  known as the *Tafsir al-Kabir*, and his influential
  philosophical and theological writings.
- **Did he discuss atomism?**
  Yes. He examined major debates about atoms, continuity,
  divisibility, and the physical structure of the world, especially in
  relation to criticisms of kalam atomism.
- **Why was his method important?**
  Because he compared arguments from different intellectual traditions
  and exposed their weaknesses with unusual technical rigor, helping
  reshape later Islamic philosophy and theology.
- **Was he completely certain about everything?**
  No simple answer is possible. Some passages associated with his
  later life express deep awareness of the limits of human certainty,
  but they should not automatically be interpreted as a complete
  rejection of philosophy.

## Why Is Fakhr al-Din al-Razi Important in the History of Philosophy?

Al-Razi is important because he was one of the most innovative
thinkers of the post-classical Islamic world. He subjected Avicennan
philosophy to sustained technical criticism while also transforming
the methods of Ash'ari theology through increasingly sophisticated
engagement with logic and philosophical argument.

His importance extends beyond criticism. Al-Razi developed distinctive
positions on questions concerning definition, essence and existence,
the principles of physics, the human soul, and the foundations of
ethical norms. His writings demonstrate that medieval Islamic
philosophy continued to develop creatively after Avicenna rather than
merely repeating earlier systems.

His work in Quranic exegesis was equally significant. Through
*Mafatih al-Ghayb*, he brought theology, philosophy, logic, and
natural inquiry into sustained conversation with scripture, creating
one of the most ambitious intellectual works in the history of Quranic
interpretation.

Fakhr al-Din al-Razi is therefore important both historically and
philosophically. He stands at a crucial point in the development of
Islamic intellectual history, where the boundaries between
**kalam and falsafa** became increasingly permeable and
where philosophical reasoning was not merely preserved, but critically
examined, transformed, and carried into new theological and
intellectual contexts.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Fakhr al-Din al-Razi

### Who was Fakhr al-Din al-Razi?

Fakhr al-Din al-Razi was a twelfth-century Islamic theologian,
philosopher, and Quranic exegete known for his critical engagement
with Avicenna's philosophy and for his monumental Quranic commentary,
the *Tafsir al-Kabir*.

### Is Fakhr al-Din al-Razi the same person as Rhazes (Abu Bakr al-Razi)?

No. Fakhr al-Din al-Razi, the Ash'ari theologian-philosopher, is a
different person from Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, known in
Latin as Rhazes, an earlier physician-philosopher. The two are
frequently confused because they share the name al-Razi but lived
roughly three centuries apart and held very different philosophical
positions.

### What is the Tafsir al-Kabir?

The *Tafsir al-Kabir*, also known as *Mafatih al-Ghayb*,
is Fakhr al-Din al-Razi's massive commentary on the Quran, notable for
incorporating extensive philosophical, theological, and scientific
discussion alongside traditional exegesis.

### How did al-Razi critique Avicenna?

Al-Razi wrote a detailed critical commentary on Avicenna's
*Remarks and Admonitions*, questioning specific arguments in
Avicenna's metaphysics and psychology, including aspects of his proof
for the Necessary Existent, while still engaging seriously with
Avicennan philosophical method.

### What is al-Razi's philosophy of atomism?

Al-Razi worked within the Ash'ari theological tradition of atomism,
which holds that the physical world is composed of indivisible atoms
and momentary accidents continuously recreated by God, an alternative
to the Aristotelian hylomorphic account of matter and form defended by
philosophers such as Avicenna.

### Did al-Razi express doubt about his own beliefs?

Yes. Toward the end of his life, al-Razi is widely reported to have
expressed philosophical and theological uncertainty, most famously in
verses lamenting that a lifetime of study in theology and philosophy
had not produced full and final certainty.

## Why Fakhr al-Din al-Razi Still Matters

Fakhr al-Din al-Razi occupies a central place in the history of
Islamic theology and philosophy as the thinker who most thoroughly
fused the methods of Ash'ari kalam with the philosophical rigor of the
Avicennan tradition, testing both against each other with
extraordinary technical precision.

His detailed critique of Avicenna, his careful treatment of atomism
and the proofs for God's existence, and his monumental
*Tafsir al-Kabir* together represent one of the most
comprehensive intellectual projects of the medieval Islamic world.

Understanding al-Razi also helps explain how later Islamic theology
absorbed and transformed the philosophical legacy of Avicenna,
Al-Ghazali, and the broader Peripatetic tradition into a distinct and
highly technical theological method.
